column2: Honoured by the other gods too with ornaments and weapons, the Goddess roared aloud with thunderous laughter again and again.
With her terrible roar the whole sky was filled, and an immense, boundless echo arose.
All the worlds were shaken, the oceans trembled, the earth quaked and all the mountains moved.
The gods joyfully cried "Victory!" to her who rides the lion, and the sages, their bodies bowed in devotion, praised her.
Seeing the three worlds all in turmoil, the enemies of the immortals marshalled all their armies and rose up with weapons raised.
Ah, what is this? cried Mahishasura in anger, and rushed toward the sound, surrounded by countless asuras.
Then he saw the Goddess pervading the three worlds with her radiance, the earth bowed beneath her tread, the sky scraped by her crown,
shaking all the netherworlds with the twang of her bowstring, standing with her thousand arms filling the directions all around.
Then began the battle between that Goddess and the enemies of the gods, the regions of space lit up by the weapons and missiles hurled in many ways.
Mahishasura's general, the great asura Chikshura, fought, and Chamara too, with others, accompanied by the fourfold army.
The great asura named Udagra fought with sixty thousand chariots, and Mahahanu with ten million.
The great asura Asiloma fought with fifty million, and Bashkala with six million in the battle.
Ugradarshana, surrounded by many thousands of elephants and horses and by ten million chariots, fought in that battle.
Bidalaksha fought in that battle surrounded by fifty million chariots.
Kala, surrounded by five hundred thousand chariots, fought in that battle, encircled by as many more.
And other great asuras there, by tens of thousands, surrounded by chariots, elephants and horses, fought in battle with the Goddess.
Mahishasura was there in the battle surrounded by thousands of crores of chariots, elephants and horses.
They fought with the Goddess in battle with javelins, bhindipalas, spears and clubs, with swords, axes and pattishas.
Some hurled spears and others nooses, and they set out to kill her with blows of their swords.
Then the Goddess Chandika, raining down her own weapons and missiles, cut those weapons and missiles to pieces as if in play.
Her face unwearied, praised by the gods and sages, the sovereign Goddess released her weapons and missiles upon the bodies of the asuras.
And the lion, the Goddess's mount, enraged, shaking its mane, stalked through the asura armies like a fire through the forests.
The breaths that Ambika released as she fought in the battle at once became her hosts, by hundreds of thousands.
Strengthened by the Goddess's power, they fought with axes, bhindipalas, swords and pattishas, destroying the hosts of asuras.
In that great festival of battle some of the hosts beat drums, others blew conches, and others played mridangas.
Then the Goddess slew the great asuras by hundreds with her trident, mace and showers of spears, and with her sword and other weapons.
Others, stunned by the sound of her bell, she struck down; and binding other asuras on the ground with her noose, she dragged them along.
Some were split in two by the sharp strokes of her sword; others, crushed by the blows of her mace, lay on the ground.
Some, badly struck by the pestle, vomited blood; some, pierced in the chest by the trident, were felled to the ground.
Some, pierced through and through by her stream of arrows on the battlefield, those tormentors of the gods, huge as mountains, gave up their lives.
Some had their arms cut off, others their necks; the heads of others fell, and others were split through the middle.
Other great asuras fell to the ground with their thighs severed; some, cut in two by the Goddess, were left with one arm, one eye and one foot.
Others, though beheaded, fell and rose again; headless trunks fought the Goddess, holding their best weapons.
Other headless trunks danced there in the battle to the rhythm of the music, swords, spears and lances in hand.
Other great asuras, their limbs drenched in streams of blood, cried out to the Goddess, "Stop, stop!" in that hair-raising battle.
The ground where that great battle took place became impassable with the fallen chariots, elephants, horses and asuras.
At once great rivers of blood flowed there amid the asura army, the elephants, asuras and horses.
In a moment Ambika brought that great army of the asuras to destruction, as fire does a great heap of grass and wood.
And the lion, roaring loudly and shaking its mane, seemed to be searching out the very lives from the bodies of the enemies of the immortals.
The Goddess and her hosts fought such a battle with the asuras there that the gods in heaven were delighted and rained down flowers.
The sage said: Having said this, she leapt up and mounted that great asura, pressed him down with her foot on his neck, and struck him with her trident.
Then he, pressed down under her foot, came halfway out of his own mouth, held fast by the Goddess's power.
Fighting while only half emerged, that great asura was felled by the Goddess, who cut off his head with her great sword.
Thus the one called Mahisha, with his army and his host of allies, who had deluded the three worlds, was destroyed by the Goddess.
When Mahisha was slain, all the beings of the three worlds — gods, asuras and men — cried out, "Victory!"
Then the whole Daitya army, crying out in dismay, perished, and all the hosts of gods attained supreme joy.
The gods, together with the divine great sages, praised the Goddess; the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the troupes of Apsaras danced.

Why do you not reduce all the asuras to ashes merely by looking at them, when you hurl your weapons at the enemies? It is so that even the enemies, purified by your weapons, may reach the higher worlds — such is your most gracious intent even toward them.
markandeypuran:81:20	That the eyes of the asuras were not destroyed by the terrible flashing of your sword's light and the radiance of your trident's point is because they looked upon your face, which is like the radiant crescent moon.
markandeypuran:81:21	Your nature, O Goddess, is to quell the conduct of the wicked; this form of yours is inconceivable and unequalled by others; your valour slays those who robbed the gods of their prowess; thus even toward enemies you have shown compassion.
markandeypuran:81:22	To what can this valour of yours be compared? Where is such beauty, which yet strikes fear into enemies? Compassion in the heart and relentlessness in battle are seen in you alone, O boon-giving Goddess, in all the three worlds.
markandeypuran:81:23	This whole threefold world has been saved by you through the destruction of the enemies; slaying them at the forefront of battle, you have led even those hosts of enemies to heaven, and removed our fear of the maddened enemies of the gods. Salutations to you.
markandeypuran:81:24	Protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambika; protect us with the sound of your bell and the twang of your bowstring.
markandeypuran:81:25	Guard us in the east and in the west, O Chandika; guard us in the south, and in the north by the whirling of your trident, O sovereign.
markandeypuran:81:26	With those gentle forms of yours that roam the three worlds, and with those exceedingly terrible ones, protect us and the earth.
markandeypuran:81:27	With the sword, trident, mace and whatever other weapons rest in your tender hands, O Ambika, protect us on every side.
The sage said: Praised thus by the gods, and worshipped with divine flowers born in Nandana and with perfumes and unguents, the upholder of the worlds,
honoured with devotion by all the thirty gods with divine incense, spoke with a gracious face to all the gods bowed before her:
The Goddess said: "Choose, all you gods, whatever you desire from me; greatly pleased, and well honoured by these hymns, I will grant it."
[The gods said:] "What else remains to be done that is difficult, we do not know." Hearing the Goddess's words, the dwellers of heaven replied:
The gods said: "Everything has been done by the Blessed One; nothing remains, since this enemy of ours, Mahishasura, has been slain.
And if you are to grant us a boon, O great sovereign, then whenever we remember you, destroy our greatest calamities.
And the mortal who praises you with these hymns, O pure-faced one, for his increase in wealth, prosperity and possessions — riches, wife and the rest — may you always be gracious, O Ambika."
The sage said: Propitiated thus by the gods for the sake of the world and themselves, Bhadrakali said, "So be it," and vanished, O king.
Thus I have told you, O king, how of old the Goddess arose from the bodies of the gods, seeking the good of the three worlds.
And again how she arose from the body of Gauri to slay the wicked Daityas, Shumbha and Nishumbha,
and to protect the worlds, benefactress of the gods — hear that from me; I will tell it to you as it happened.
To the Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of the mother, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
To the Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of illusion, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.
To her who presides over the senses of all beings and ever pervades all beings, to the all-pervading Goddess, salutations again and again.
To her who, in the form of consciousness, abides pervading this whole world, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations to her, salutations again and again.

Praised of old by the gods for the fulfilment of their wishes, and served on many days by the lord of the gods, may that sovereign, the cause of good, bring us auspicious and blessed things and strike down our calamities.
She who is now worshipped by us gods, tormented by the arrogant Daityas, and who, when remembered by those bowed in devotion, at that very moment destroys all our calamities.
The sage said: As the gods were thus engaged in hymns and the like, Parvati came there to bathe in the waters of the Jahnavi, O prince.
The fair-browed one said to those gods, "Whom are you praising here?" And Shiva, arising from the sheath of her body, said:
This hymn is addressed to me by the gods, driven out by the Daitya Shumbha and defeated in battle by Nishumbha.

This celestial car yoked with swans, a jewel brought here, which was Brahma's marvel, stands in your courtyard.
markandeypuran:82:52	This great treasure, the Mahapadma, has been brought from the lord of wealth, and the ocean gave a garland of unfading lotuses with their filaments.
markandeypuran:82:53	Varuna's umbrella, which pours down gold, stands in your house, and this best of chariots that once belonged to Prajapati.
markandeypuran:82:54	The spear of Death called Utkrantida has been taken by you, O lord, and the noose of the king of waters is in your brother's possession.
markandeypuran:82:55	All the kinds of jewels born of the ocean belong to Nishumbha; and Fire too gave you two garments purified by fire.
markandeypuran:82:56	Thus, O lord of Daityas, all jewels have been brought to you; why do you not take this auspicious one, the jewel among women?
The sage said: Hearing these words of Chanda and Munda, the great asura Shumbha sent Sugriva as messenger to the Goddess.
Shumbha said: "Go and tell her such and such at my word; act quickly so that she comes gladly."
He went to where she was on the very beautiful mountain slope, and spoke to the Goddess gently in a sweet voice.
The messenger said: "Goddess, Shumbha, lord of the Daityas, is the supreme lord in the three worlds; I am a messenger sent by him, and have come here to you.
His command is never obstructed among any of the races of gods, and he has conquered all the enemies of the Daityas; hear what he says:
'The whole three worlds are mine, and the gods are obedient to me; I enjoy all the shares of sacrifice separately.
All the finest jewels in the three worlds are in my power; likewise the jewel among elephants, the mount of the king of gods, which I seized.
The jewel among horses called Ucchaihshravas, born from the churning of the ocean of milk, was offered to me by the immortals, bowing down.
Whatever other things were jewels among the gods, Gandharvas and serpents are now with me, lovely one.
We consider you, Goddess, the jewel among women in the world; so come to us, since we are the enjoyers of jewels.
Take me or my younger brother, Nishumbha of great valour, O you with restless glances, for you are indeed a jewel.
By becoming mine you will obtain supreme, incomparable lordship; consider this with your understanding and become my wife.'"
The sage said: Addressed thus, the Goddess smiled inwardly and spoke gravely — Durga, the blessed and auspicious one, by whom this world is upheld.
The Goddess said: "You have spoken the truth; nothing you have said is false. Shumbha is lord of the three worlds, and Nishumbha is likewise.
But how can I make false the vow I have made in this matter? Hear the vow I made long ago out of little understanding:
'He who conquers me in battle, who removes my pride, who is my equal in strength in the world — he shall be my husband.'
So let Shumbha come here, or the great asura Nishumbha; let him conquer me and take my hand quickly — why delay?"
The messenger said: "You are arrogant, Goddess; do not speak so before me. What man in the three worlds could stand before Shumbha and Nishumbha?
All the gods cannot stand face to face in battle even with the other Daityas, Goddess; how much less you, a lone woman?
Shumbha and the others, before whom Indra and all the gods could not stand in battle — how will you, a woman, face them?
So go, as I tell you, to Shumbha and Nishumbha; do not go with your dignity destroyed by being dragged by the hair."
The Goddess said: "So it is: Shumbha is mighty and Nishumbha exceedingly valiant. What can I do, since my vow was made long ago without reflection?
So go and tell all this that I have said, respectfully, to the lord of the asuras; and let him do what is fitting."
In a moment that whole army was destroyed by the great-souled lion, the Goddess's exceedingly wrathful mount.
Hearing that the asura Dhumralochana had been slain by the Goddess, and his whole army destroyed by the Goddess's lion,
Shumbha, lord of the Daityas, grew angry, his lip quivering, and commanded the two great asuras Chanda and Munda:

O Chanda, O Munda, surrounded by many forces, go there, and having gone, bring her quickly,
markandeypuran:83:19	dragging her by the hair or binding her; and if you have any doubt about the fight, then let her be slain by all the asuras with all their weapons.
markandeypuran:83:20	When that wicked one has been slain and the lion struck down, then bind that Ambika, seize her, and come back quickly.
Likewise, putting warriors, horses, and chariots with their charioteers into her mouth, she chewed them most terribly with her teeth.
She seized one by the hair and another by the neck; she trampled another with her foot and crushed another against her breast.
The weapons and great missiles hurled by those asuras she caught in her mouth in anger and ground them with her teeth.
She crushed the whole army of those mighty, evil-souled asuras; some she devoured and others she struck down.
Some were slain by the sword, some beaten with the khatvanga; asuras perished in the battle struck by the points of her teeth.
Seeing that great army of asuras felled in a moment, Chanda rushed at that most terrible Kali.
The great asura covered that fearful-eyed one with showers of most terrible arrows, and Munda with discuses hurled by the thousand.
Those many discuses entering her mouth shone like many orbs of the sun entering the belly of a cloud.
Then Kali, roaring terribly, laughed fiercely in great anger, her dreadful mouth gleaming with fearful teeth.
Mounting her great lion, the Goddess rushed at Chanda, seized him by the hair and cut off his head with her sword.
When his head was cut off, the lord of Daityas gave a most terrible cry, and the three worlds were terrified by that great cry.
Then Munda, seeing Chanda felled, rushed at her; and she in anger struck him down to the ground with her sword.
Then the remnant of the army, seeing Chanda and the mighty Munda felled, fled in all directions, stricken with fear.
Kali, taking the head of Chanda and of Munda, went to Chandika and said, with fierce loud laughter:
I have brought you here Chanda and Munda, two great beasts; in the sacrifice of battle you yourself will slay Shumbha and Nishumbha.
The sage said: Seeing the two great asuras Chanda and Munda brought there, the auspicious Chandika spoke gracious words to Kali:
The Goddess said: "Since you have come bringing Chanda and Munda, you shall be famed in the world as Chamunda, O Goddess."
Whatever form each god had, with ornaments and mount to match, in that very form his Shakti came to fight the asuras.
In a celestial car yoked with swans, bearing a rosary and water-pot, came the Shakti of Brahma; she is called Brahmani.
Maheshvari came riding a bull, holding a fine trident, with great serpents for bracelets and adorned with the crescent moon.
Kaumari, spear in hand, riding the best of peacocks, came to fight the Daityas — Ambika in the form of Guha.
Likewise the Shakti of Vishnu came, seated on Garuda, holding conch, discus, mace, bow and sword.
The Shakti of Hari who bears the incomparable form of the boar came there too, bearing the body of Varahi.
Narasimhi came there, bearing a body like Narasimha's, scattering the hosts of stars with the tossing of her mane.
Likewise Aindri came, thunderbolt in hand, seated on the king of elephants, thousand-eyed, just like Shakra.
Then Ishana, surrounded by those Shaktis of the gods, said to Chandika, "Let the asuras be slain quickly, for my pleasure."
Then from the Goddess's body came forth the most terrible Shakti of Chandika, exceedingly fierce, howling like a hundred jackals.
And that invincible one said to Ishana of smoky matted locks, "Go as messenger, blessed one, to Shumbha and Nishumbha.
Tell Shumbha and Nishumbha, the exceedingly proud Danavas, and the other Danavas gathered there for battle:
'Let Indra have the three worlds and let the gods enjoy the oblations; you go to Patala if you wish to live.
But if in the pride of your strength you are eager for battle, then come, and let my jackals be sated with your flesh.'"
Because Shiva himself was appointed as messenger by that Goddess, she became famous in this world as Shivaduti.
The great asuras, hearing the Goddess's words as told by Sharva, went full of indignation to where Katyayani stood.
Then at the very outset the enemies of the immortals, in their arrogant fury, rained arrows, spears and lances on the Goddess.
And she, with great arrows shot from her drawn bow, cut down as in play those arrows, tridents, spears and axes hurled at her.
Before her Kali roamed, tearing enemies with the strokes of her trident and crushing them with her khatvanga.
Wherever Brahmani ran, she made the enemies powerless and lustreless by sprinkling water from her water-pot.
Maheshvari slew the Daityas with her trident, Vaishnavi with her discus, and Kaumari, exceedingly wrathful, with her spear.
By the fall of Aindri's thunderbolt, Daityas and Danavas by the hundred fell torn to the ground, pouring out streams of blood.
Shattered by blows of the snout, their chests wounded by the tips of the tusks, and torn by the discus, they fell before the boar-formed one.
Narasimhi roamed the battle devouring other great asuras torn by her claws, filling the regions of space with her roaring.
Unnerved by Shivaduti's fierce laughter, the asuras fell to the earth, and she then devoured those who had fallen.
Seeing the enraged host of Mothers crushing the great asuras by various means, the soldiers of the gods' enemies fled.
Seeing the Daityas harassed by the host of Mothers and bent on flight, the great asura Raktabija came forward in anger to fight.
Whenever a drop of blood from his body falls to the ground, a great asura of his size springs up from the earth.
The great asura fought, mace in hand, with Indra's Shakti; then Aindri struck Raktabija with her thunderbolt.
Struck by the thunderbolt, he quickly shed much blood; from it arose warriors of his form and his prowess.
As many drops of blood fell from his body, so many men were born, with his valour, strength and prowess.
Those men born of the blood fought there with the Mothers, most terribly, hurling fearsome weapons.
And again, when his head was wounded by the fall of the thunderbolt, blood flowed, and from it men were born by the thousand.
Vaishnavi struck him in battle with her discus, and Aindri beat that lord of asuras with her mace.
The world was filled with thousands of great asuras of his size, born from the blood flowing from him when cut by Vaishnavi's discus.
Kaumari struck the great asura Raktabija with her spear, Varahi with her sword, and Maheshvari with her trident.
And that Daitya, the great asura Raktabija, filled with rage, struck each of the Mothers separately with his mace.
From the stream of blood that fell to the ground from him, struck many times by spears, tridents and the rest, asuras arose by the hundred.
The whole world was pervaded by those asuras born of the asura's blood, and the gods fell into the greatest fear.
Seeing the gods dejected, Chandika quickly said to Kali, "Chamunda, open wide your mouth;
with this swift mouth take in the drops of blood, and the great asuras born of the drops of blood when my weapons strike him.
Roam the battle devouring the great asuras born of them; thus this Daitya, drained of blood, will perish; and devoured by you, no other fierce ones will arise."
The sage said: Having said this to her, the Goddess struck him with her trident, and Kali took Raktabija's blood into her mouth.
Then he struck Chandika there with his mace, but the blow of the mace caused her not the slightest pain.
From his wounded body much blood flowed, and wherever it flowed Chamunda caught it in her mouth.
The great asuras that sprang up in her mouth from the falling blood Chamunda devoured, and she drank his blood.
The Goddess slew Raktabija, whose blood had been drunk by Chamunda, with trident, discus, arrows, swords and lances.
Struck by the mass of weapons, the great asura Raktabija fell to the ground, bloodless, O king.
Then the gods attained incomparable joy, O king, and the host of Mothers born from them danced, intoxicated with blood.
The Goddess cut down the arrows Shumbha shot, and Shumbha the arrows she sent, with fierce arrows of their own, by hundreds and thousands.
Then Chandika in anger struck him with her trident; struck by it, he fell unconscious to the ground.
Then Nishumbha, regaining consciousness and taking up his bow, struck the Goddess, Kali and the lion with arrows.
Again that lord of Danavas, the son of Diti, making ten thousand arms, covered Chandika with discuses.
Then the blessed Durga, destroyer of the distress of difficulties, in anger cut down those discuses and those arrows with her own arrows.
Then Nishumbha, surrounded by the Daitya army, seized his mace and rushed swiftly at Chandika to kill her.
As he was rushing at her, Chandika quickly cut his mace with her sharp-edged sword, and he took up a trident.
As Nishumbha, tormentor of the immortals, came on with trident in hand, Chandika pierced him in the heart with her swiftly hurled trident.
From the heart of him pierced by the trident came out another man, of great strength and valour, crying, "Stop!"
As he emerged, the Goddess laughed aloud and cut off his head with her sword; then he fell to the ground.
Then the lion devoured those fierce asuras whose necks it had crushed with its fangs, and Kali and Shivaduti devoured others.
Some great asuras perished pierced by Kaumari's spear; others were driven off by water purified by Brahmani's mantras.
Others fell pierced by Maheshvari's trident; some were ground to powder on the earth by blows of Varahi's snout.
Danavas were cut to pieces by Vaishnavi's discus, and others by the thunderbolt hurled from the tip of Aindri's hand.
Some asuras perished, some fled from the great battle, and others were devoured by Kali, Shivaduti and the lion.
O eternal one, who are the power of creation, preservation and destruction, the abode of the qualities and made of the qualities, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you intent on rescuing the helpless and afflicted who take refuge in you, O Goddess who remove the suffering of all, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you seated in a car yoked with swans, bearing the form of Brahmani, sprinkling water with kusha grass, O Goddess, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you who bear the trident, the moon and the serpent, riding the great bull, in the form of Maheshvari, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O sinless one, attended by peacocks and cocks, bearing the great spear, abiding in the form of Kaumari, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you who hold the supreme weapons — conch, discus, mace and the bow Sharnga — be gracious, O you in the form of Vaishnavi, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you who hold the fierce great discus and lifted up the earth on your tusk, O auspicious one in the form of the boar, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you who in the fierce form of Narasimha strove to slay the Daityas, bent on saving the three worlds, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O crowned one with the great thunderbolt, blazing with a thousand eyes, taker of Vritra's life, O Aindri, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you who in the form of Shivaduti slew the mighty host of Daityas, of terrible form and great roar, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you whose face is terrible with fangs, adorned with a garland of heads, O Chamunda, crusher of Munda, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O Lakshmi, Modesty, Great Knowledge, Faith, Nourishment, Svadha, Constancy, Great Night, Great Illusion, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O Intelligence, Sarasvati, excellent one, Prosperity, tawny one, dark one, Destiny — be gracious, O sovereign, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you with hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere, with ears and noses everywhere, O Narayani, salutations to you.
O you whose form is all, sovereign of all, endowed with all powers, protect us from fears, O Goddess; O Goddess Durga, salutations to you.
May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all fears; O Katyayani, salutations to you.
May your trident, terrible with flames, exceedingly fierce, destroyer of all asuras, protect us from fear; O Bhadrakali, salutations to you.
May that bell of yours which, filling the world with its sound, destroys the might of the Daityas, protect us from sins, O Goddess, as a mother protects her children.
May your sword, gleaming in your hand and smeared with the mire of the asuras' blood and fat, be for our good; O Chandika, we bow to you.

When pleased you destroy all diseases, but when angered you destroy all the desires one longs for. For men who have taken refuge in you there is no calamity; those who take refuge in you become a refuge for others.
This slaughter that you have wrought today of the great asuras who hate dharma, O Goddess, by making your own form manifold in many shapes, O Ambika — what other goddess could do that?

In the branches of knowledge, in the scriptures that are lamps of discrimination, and in the primordial words, who but you? And you whirl this universe about in the pit of possessiveness, in the deepest darkness.

Where there are rakshasas, where there are serpents of virulent poison, where there are enemies and hordes of robbers, where there is forest fire, and in the midst of the ocean — there you stand and protect the universe.

O sovereign of the universe, you protect the universe; as the soul of the universe you uphold it; you are worthy of the worship of the lord of the universe, and those who bow to you in devotion become the refuge of the universe.

O Goddess, be gracious; protect us always from fear of enemies, just as you have done now by slaying the asuras; and quickly bring to peace the sins of all the worlds and the great calamities born of the ripening of evil portents.

Be gracious, O Goddess, to those who bow to you, you who remove the afflictions of the universe; O you who are worthy of praise by the dwellers of the three worlds, be the giver of boons to the worlds."
The Goddess said: "I am the giver of boons, O host of gods; choose the boon you desire in your hearts, beneficial to the worlds, and I will grant it."
The gods said: "O sovereign of all, in this very way may you quell all the afflictions of the three worlds and destroy our enemies."
The Goddess said: "When the Vaivasvata period has come, in the twenty-eighth age, two other great asuras, Shumbha and Nishumbha, will arise.
Born in the house of the cowherd Nanda, from the womb of Yashoda, dwelling on the Vindhya mountain, I will then destroy them.
And again, descending to earth in a most fierce form, I will slay the Danavas descended from Viprachitti.
As I devour those fierce Danavas of Viprachitti's line, my teeth will become red like pomegranate flowers;
then the gods in heaven and men in the world of mortals, praising me, will always call me Raktadantika (red-toothed).
And again, when there is a drought of a hundred years without water, praised by the sages I will be born on earth, not from a womb.
Then, since I will look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, men will celebrate me as Shatakshi (hundred-eyed).
Then, O gods, I will sustain the whole world with life-sustaining vegetables born of my own body, until the rains come;
then I will become famous on earth as Shakambhari. And there I will slay the great asura called Durgama, and my name will become famous as the Goddess Durga.
And again, when I take a terrible form on the Himalaya and devour the rakshasas to protect the sages,
then all the sages will praise me with bodies bowed, and my name will become famous as the Goddess Bhima.
When the one called Aruna causes great affliction in the three worlds, then I will take the form of countless bees
and slay the great asura for the good of the three worlds; then people everywhere will praise me as Bhramari.
Thus, whenever affliction arises from the Danavas, then I will descend and destroy the enemies."

At the great annual worship performed in autumn, whoever hears this greatness of mine with devotion
markandeypuran:89:12	will be freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth and grain by my grace; there is no doubt.
markandeypuran:89:13	By hearing this greatness of mine, and my auspicious manifestations, and my prowess in battles, a man becomes fearless.

The sage said: Having said this, the blessed Chandika of fierce valour vanished right there as the gods looked on.
And the gods, free from fear, their enemies slain, all resumed their offices as before, enjoying their shares of sacrifice.

And when Shumbha, the enemy of the gods and destroyer of the world, of exceedingly fierce and incomparable valour, and the mighty Nishumbha had been slain in battle by the Goddess, the remaining Daityas went to Patala.
Thus the blessed Goddess, though eternal, arises again and again, O king, and protects the world.
By her this universe is deluded, and she herself gives birth to the universe; when entreated she grants knowledge, and when pleased, prosperity.
This whole cosmic egg is pervaded by her, O lord of men — by Mahakali, who at the time of the great dissolution takes the form of the great destroyer.
At the proper time she is the great pestilence, and she, the unborn, becomes creation; she, the eternal, sustains beings in their time.
In times of prosperity she is Lakshmi in men's homes, granting increase; and in times of want she becomes Alakshmi, bringing ruin.
Praised and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes and the like, she grants wealth and sons, a mind set on dharma, and an auspicious destiny.
When the two, self-controlled, had worshipped her thus for three years, Chandika, upholder of the world, well pleased, appeared before them and spoke.
The Goddess said: "Whatever you ask, O king, and you, joy of your family, receive it all from me; well pleased, I grant it."
Markandeya said: Then the king chose a kingdom that would not be lost in another birth, and in this very life his own kingdom, with the power of his enemies destroyed by force.
And the merchant, whose mind was disenchanted with the world, wisely chose the knowledge that removes attachment, the sense of 'mine' and 'I.'
The Goddess said: "In a few days, O king, you will regain your own kingdom; having slain your enemies, it will remain secure for you.
And when you die, you will be born again from the god Vivasvat, and will be a Manu on earth named Savarnika.
Best of merchants, the boon you desired from me I grant for your perfection: you will have knowledge."
Markandeya said: Having granted each of them the boon they desired, the Goddess, praised by them with devotion, at once vanished.
Thus, having obtained the boon from the Goddess, Suratha, bull among kshatriyas, taking birth from the Sun, will become Savarni Manu.
[The deities], radiant with all ornaments, should be worshipped with care; the guardians of the worlds should be worshipped as before, and likewise the thunderbolt and other weapons.
The wise one should recite it sixteen lakh times and offer oblations of a tenth of that with ghee into a fire of khadira wood; then the mantra becomes perfected.
Offering ten thousand oblations of lotuses, one brings a king under one's control; offering blue lotuses, great prosperity surely arises.
Offering palasha flowers for a year, one becomes a poet; by an oblation of mustard and salt one brings a woman under one's control.
Having enjoyed pleasures on earth, at the end one reaches Vishnu's world — one devoted to the japa of the seed-syllable of speech; there is no need to doubt this.
Having offered a seat with this, one should form the image with the root mantra and worship the Goddess duly; now the procedure is described.
Tara (Om), Maya (Hrim), Bhaga, Brahma, jate, the sun with a long vowel, 'to the lord of Yakshas,' and then 'this offering brought with diligence' —
'take, take, Shiva, svaha' — this is declared to be the offering mantra. With it one should give an offering daily at midnight at a crossroads.
Then one should perform the giving of water and the like with ten mantras: the dhruva (Om), 'vajrodake,' the armour syllable, and 'phat' — the seven-syllable mantra for taking water.
Beginning with Tara and ending with the wife of Fire (svaha), with Maya, is held to be for washing; Tara, Maya, Bhrigu, ear, 'vishuddham,' 'dharma' with the armour syllable —
'all sins are pacified,' 'chhe' with the eye syllable and water; 'kalpanta-nayana svaha' is held to be the mantra for sipping water.
The dhruva, then 'manidhari' at the end, 'vajrini' with the eye syllable and 'mriti,' 'khari,' 'vidya'... at the end of 'sarva,' baka with abja —
'karini' at the end, the long armour syllable, the weapon syllable and ending with the beloved of Fire — this twenty-three-syllable mantra is for tying the topknot.
The pranava, 'raksha' twice, the long armour syllable, the weapon syllable and two 'tha's — with this nine-syllable mantra the practitioner should purify the ground.
After 'nara,' the words 'sarvavighnan utsaraya,' then 'hum phat svaha' — this mantra of thirty-one syllables removes obstacles.
One should meditate on the Maya seed-syllable, like a hibiscus flower, at the navel, and with the fire arising from it burn the body together with one's sins.
The knower of mantras should meditate on the Tara seed-syllable, golden in colour, in the heart, and with the wind arising from it scatter the ashes of sin onto the ground.
Meditating on the fourth seed-syllable, like the moon or jasmine, at the forehead, with the nectar arising from it one's body becomes like that of the deity.
By this purification of the elements one attains likeness to the Goddess. Tara, Ananta, Bhrigu, ear, joined with Padmanabha and Bali,
'khe vajrarekhe,' the seed called Krodha, and the beloved of Fire — with this twelve-syllable mantra one should draw an auspicious mandala.
Tara, 'yathagata,' Nidra, with ri and ka, Bhrigu, visha, with the long vowel, smriti, au with the eye syllable, Mahakala with bha,
Krodha and the weapon syllable — this mantra of fourteen syllables is for purifying flowers and the like. Tara, Pasha, Para, svaha — the five-syllable one is for purifying the mind.
Ten mantras have been declared; now the placing of the arghya is described. With Maya joined to the two moons from the month, create the earth-square,

a circle joined with a triangle — one should make the mandala with the mantra and worship there the supporting power in the middle of the fire-mandala; having worshipped the fire-mandala, one should place the great conch.
With the sky syllable joined with the left ear and the moon, ending in 'phat,' one should wash it, and recite Bhrigu with the staff, joined with the three forms.
Then one should worship the great conch reciting four mantras: Maya with three long vowels, Kali, Srishti with long 'sa,'
'masam' joined with Pratima, Yavana, then the heart syllable — this eleven-syllable mantra is the first for worshipping the great conch.
Hamsa joined with Hari and the lord of serpents, with three long vowels and the moon, 'tarini' at the end, 'kapalaya namah' — the twelve-syllable mantra.
'Sva' with three long vowels, this with the left eye, 'lokapalaya' and the heart syllable — this is the third, the syllable of Shiva.
